clue.text: Tip: borstal may be what he needs

definitions.text: Tip: borstal may be what he needs

indicators.note: 'May be' offers the letters as one possible arrangement rather than the one printed, which is the licence to reorder them.

parts.note: three letters of fodder, the piece of advice being offered
seven more, from the name of the British reformatory for young offenders, abolished in 1982

explanation.surface: A word of advice: the lad in question might benefit from a spell in a young offenders' institution.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: the sentence is advice about a badly brought-up boy, and its first two words are also the letters he is made of. Only 'may be' hints that they need rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue describes a child so indulged that a stretch in borstal looks like the cure, which is exactly who the answer names.

clue.text: Representation of the USA by pawnbrokers before midday

parts.note: uncle is old British slang for a pawnbroker, the man you take your watch to when funds run short
a.m. is ante meridiem, Latin for before midday

explanation.surface: A picture of America turned out by pawnbrokers in the course of a morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural is the giveaway that the first word is not family: pawnbrokers have been called uncles since the eighteenth century. The top-hatted figure himself dates from the war of 1812.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the national personification of the United States, the pointing figure of the 'I Want You' recruiting poster.

clue.text: Several folk snorkelling

definitions.meaning: an old adjective for various or sundry, still met in legal and biblical English
people who take themselves under the water, which is what anyone with a snorkel is doing

explanation.surface: A few people out in the bay with snorkels.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently — DYE-vers for the swimmers, DIVE-ers for the old word meaning various — and nothing in the clue tells you which comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means various or sundry, and the same six letters are simply people who dive, which snorkellers do.

clue.text: Australian group is overabundant, we're told

indicators.note: What we are told reaches us as a sound, so the letters written down only have to match the noise, not the spelling.

parts.note: anything overabundant is in excess, and the band spelt that phrase as letters to be read out

explanation.surface: Word has it that a certain band from Australia is far too much of a good thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is meant to be said, not read: four letters pronounced one after another give the phrase back. Michael Hutchence fronted the Sydney six-piece through the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: INXS were the Sydney rock band behind 'Need You Tonight', so the definition names them by nationality and kind.

clue.text: Danger is spoken of in style of radiological machine

indicators.note: What is spoken of arrives as a noise rather than as spelling, so what goes down on paper is a different way of writing the same sound.

parts.note: the manner of doing a thing is the style it is done in; these six letters open after the first

indicators.note: What happens in something happens inside it, so the piece just heard is set within the letters of the word that follows.

parts.note: a danger is a risk, and said aloud that is also RISC, the reduced instruction set computing used in chip design

explanation.surface: Talk about the danger, conducted with a certain elegance.
explanation.walkthrough: The chip architecture is the only spelling of that sound that fits, and 'in style' is not a compliment but an instruction to plant it inside. Scanner then falls out of a word for style that nobody expects to be split.
explanation.definitionFit: An MRI scanner is the tube a patient slides into in a hospital's radiology department, imaging the body with magnets where an X-ray machine uses radiation.

clue.text: Wholesale trader with Ivory's film partner

definitions.meaning: one who buys and sells in bulk rather than over a shop counter
James Ivory directed; his producer of forty years is the other half of the partnership behind A Room with a View

explanation.surface: A bulk dealer who also happens to be the film-maker's business partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivory looks like the material a trader might deal in, which is the whole trap; it is the surname of the American director. Ismail, the producer, died in 2005 after forty-four years of the partnership.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant is a trader dealing wholesale, and Ismail Merchant was James Ivory's producing partner, their names joined on every film they made.

clue.text: Santa likely, initially, to move cautiously on it?

definitions.text: Santa likely, initially, to move cautiously on it?

indicators.note: What is done initially is done at the very start, so each of the words named gives up only its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of the name
the next word's first letter, taken the same way
to edge somewhere is to go a little at a time, feeling your way

explanation.surface: Father Christmas setting off gingerly on his runners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' works on two words at once, and what is left of the sentence is a picture of the man himself. The clue defines the vehicle by describing the ride rather than naming it, which is what the question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue pictures Santa inching along on the runnered thing he travels by, and 'it' is that vehicle.

clue.text: It's ours to bear!

parts.note: a weight you bear is one resting on you
whatever is ours belongs to us

explanation.surface: A burden that falls to the whole of us to carry.
explanation.walkthrough: Split after two letters the answer says in little words what the sentence says in long ones: it is on us. The word came into English straight from the Latin for a load, and law still uses it that way.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is the duty or burden that falls to you, so the whole clue reads straight: a thing that is ours and has to be carried.

clue.text: Old fellow at French guest-house outside of Exeter

parts.note: a pension is the French boarding house that puts you up and feeds you

indicators.note: The outside of a word is its two ends, so the first and last letters stay and everything between them is dropped.

parts.note: the outer letters of the Devon city's name

explanation.surface: An elderly gentleman staying at a small boarding house just beyond the city limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside of Exeter' sounds like a map reference and is a letter instruction. The French word is the same one that gives us the retirement payment, which is where the definition comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A pensioner is someone living on a retirement pension, so 'old fellow' points at the answer by the age at which one is drawn.

clue.text: Somewhat well-endowed woman

indicators.note: Somewhat means to a limited extent, so only part of what follows is wanted — a run of letters inside it rather than the whole.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken from inside the first half of the word into the second

explanation.surface: A woman generously provided for.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen is there to stop your eye at the wrong place; the run of letters straddles it. 'Somewhat' is the only word in the clue doing any instructing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen is an ordinary English woman's name, so the definition names the answer by its kind rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Complaint from one head about pupils

indicators.note: To go about a thing is to pass round it, so the letters already gathered close on either side of what comes next.

parts.note: the single stroke that counts as one in Roman numerals
a ness is a headland, the piece of coast that juts out — Orford Ness, Sheerness
a learner shows an L-plate, and two of them give the letter twice

explanation.surface: A head teacher grumbling about the children in the school.
explanation.walkthrough: The head is a coastal one, not the one in the staffroom, and 'about' is where the two pieces part company to let the learners in. English coastal names are full of the word: Dungeness, Skegness, Fifeness.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is what a doctor calls the thing you have come in with, the same everyday sense as the answer.

clue.text: Short time before new seed withdraws

indicators.note: What is new is not what was there before, so those letters come out in an arrangement of their own.
Short asks for the cut-down form of the word beside it, the one that stops before the end is reached.

parts.note: a second is a unit of time, and this is what survives when the word is cut down
the four letters of the word in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Not long after being planted, a new seed backs out of the whole business.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a gardening scene that cannot happen, which is the signal that 'new' is not describing the seed but shuffling it. Secession is what a state does when it leaves a union.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to withdraw formally from a union or federation, so the definition is the plain verb in the same third-person form.

clue.text: Trout-fishing river's matches

parts.note: the Test is the Hampshire chalk stream that is England's most famous trout water
the possessive ending hands over its own letter

explanation.surface: Fixtures belonging to a river where the trout fishing is good.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe reads as possession and is really the join between two pieces. Test matches are cricket's five-day internationals, so both halves of the clue are things an English summer is made of.
explanation.definitionFit: Tests are the five-day internationals of cricket, the plural everyone uses for them without the word 'match' at all.

clue.text: Limeys from a distant place amongst spectators

indicators.note: To be amongst others is to stand in the middle of them, so these letters are set inside the ones already found.

parts.note: those who see, watching whatever is put in front of them; the five letters open after two
afar is where anything distant is seen from

explanation.surface: British sailors arriving from somewhere remote and lost in the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectators' is the word to crack: the short synonym for them is usually met meaning a prophet, and it is only doing its literal job here.
explanation.definitionFit: Limey began as American slang for a British sailor, the Royal Navy having issued lime juice against scurvy, so it names the answer by its best-known sort.

clue.text: Flower and photo by fierce type

parts.note: a snap is a photograph, the quick informal kind
a dragon is what a formidable, fire-breathing sort of person gets called

explanation.surface: A bloom and a photograph, both down to somebody fearsome.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces are the plant's own etymology: the bloom has jaws that open when you squeeze its sides and snap shut when you let go.
explanation.definitionFit: The snapdragon is the cottage-garden antirrhinum, so 'flower' names it by the plainest possible category.

clue.text: Dumbfounded there is no address?

parts.note: an address is what is delivered from a podium, not what goes on an envelope
having none of a thing is the ending that says it is absent

explanation.surface: Struck dumb on discovering that no address has been given.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is the envelope: 'address' wants to be a street and a number, and it is the thing given from a podium. The question mark is the setter admitting that a suffix has been built out of an ordinary word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be speechless is to be so astonished that nothing comes out, which is exactly what dumbfounded describes.

clue.text: 1964 horror fantasy film of Lazio playing the A.S. team?

definitions.meaning: an Italian picture of that year, sold in English-speaking countries as War of the Zombies
Lazio and AS Roma are the two clubs of a single city, so a derby between them sets that city against itself

explanation.surface: A cheap 1964 horror picture that turns out to be a football fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same phrase read differently. Lazio and AS Roma share the Stadio Olimpico, so the derby really is one half of a capital city playing the other; the film is Roma contro Roma, legionaries against the undead.
explanation.definitionFit: Rome Against Rome is the English title of the 1964 Italian horror Roma contro Roma, and the phrase equally describes the capital's derby, one of its clubs against the other.

clue.text: One no longer believing in a job caused worry

parts.note: the article used as it stands
a post is a position of employment
what eats at a person is what gnaws away at them — 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: A position at work that turned out to be a source of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like an instruction to put something inside and is only joinery. The word is Greek for one who stands away, and it is stronger than 'doubter': it means a believer who has left.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate is someone who has renounced the faith they once held, so the definition is a person who no longer believes.

clue.text: The Spectator or Sunday newspaper

definitions.meaning: set in italics to look like the weekly magazine, though it is only a person watching
the broadsheet founded in 1791, the oldest Sunday paper in the world

explanation.surface: A choice between the weekly magazine and one of the Sunday papers.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics are the whole trick: they dress an ordinary noun as a masthead, so the clue reads as two publications when the first is a common word for anyone who watches.
explanation.definitionFit: An observer is one who watches, which is what a spectator is; and The Observer is Britain's Sunday broadsheet, so the same word answers both halves.

clue.text: Giant Carmelites, perhaps, too much to expect

indicators.note: Perhaps says the thing named is only one instance of something wider, so what is wanted is the class the friars belong to.

parts.note: as an adjective, giant describes something of unusual height
the Carmelites are one of the Catholic religious orders, the white friars founded on Mount Carmel

explanation.surface: Carmelite friars of remarkable height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' wants to be a noun and has to be read as a size. The phrase itself comes from the theatre and shop trade, where an order too large to fill was a tall one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall order is a demand that can hardly be met, which is what asking too much to expect amounts to.

clue.text: General method to establish latitude

parts.note: Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederate armies, and crossword generals are nearly always him
the way a thing is done is the method used

explanation.surface: A broadly applicable technique for working out how far north you are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' reads as an adjective covering 'method' and is a man. The sailing sense underneath is a ship's sideways drift, which is where the room-to-manoeuvre meaning comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is the margin you have to play with, and latitude carries the same figurative sense of freedom to act, not the line on a map the surface offers.

clue.text: Sounds essential but cut short, I see

definitions.note: Music is a mass noun and 'sounds' a plural, but the plural is the ordinary way of speaking about what fills the air when it is played.

indicators.note: To cut something short is to stop it before its end, so the word loses its final letter.

parts.note: what is essential is a must, and the word arrives with its tail lopped off
the letter as written
C is the letter spoken exactly as this word, a standing crossword equivalence

explanation.surface: Something indispensable, though not at full length, as far as I can tell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' at the front looks like an instruction to listen for a homophone; it is the definition, and nothing in this clue is heard rather than read. The trailing 'I see' is two separate pieces, not a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Music is organised sound, so the definition names it by the raw material rather than by any of its forms.

clue.text: Craftsmen for two generations

parts.note: the older of the two named: ma is mother
the younger, following straight on

explanation.surface: A family firm that has kept going for a couple of generations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two generations' reads as a stretch of time and is a list of people instead: a parent and her children, written one after the other. Stonemasons really did pass the trade down that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Masons are the craftsmen who cut and lay stone, so the definition is the trade in its plural.

clue.text: In real trouble, shock treatment for sort of complex

indicators.note: In places one thing within another, so the piece named after the comma is planted inside the letters this word introduces.
Something in trouble is not in good order, so the letters beside it are not to be taken in the order given.

parts.note: the four letters of the word in a new order, opening after the first two
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, the shock treatment of psychiatric wards

explanation.surface: Somebody in serious difficulty and receiving shock therapy for a psychological condition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is so medically coherent that the fodder hides in plain sight — 'real' is not describing the trouble, it is the material being shuffled. Jung named the complex after the daughter who urged the killing of her mother.
explanation.definitionFit: The Electra complex is the name given to a daughter's rivalry with her mother for her father, the female counterpart of the Oedipus complex.

clue.text: Nobleman nearly at the centre

indicators.note: What sits at the centre is what is left once both ends have been taken away.

parts.note: the word loses its first and last letters and what remains is the middle four

explanation.surface: A peer standing not quite in the middle of the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' looks like a qualifier softening 'at the centre' and is the word being operated on. An earl ranks third in the British peerage, below a marquess and above a viscount.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a member of the British peerage, so the definition names the answer by its rank in the simplest terms.

clue.text: Straw breaking camel's back, doubly profligate

indicators.note: Something broken comes apart, and the bits can be put back together in any order.

parts.note: the five letters of the word in a new order

indicators.note: The back of a word is its end, and 'doubly' asks for two letters of that end rather than the single one usually wanted.

parts.note: the last two letters of the animal's name

explanation.surface: The final straw landing on an already overloaded camel.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb about the last straw makes the clue read as one phrase, which is why the two halves are hard to separate: one is fodder and the other supplies just two letters. Nothing here is breaking a back.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel is someone who squanders money, time and chances alike, which is what calling a person a profligate means.

clue.text: Heartless worries!

indicators.note: Something heartless has had its middle taken out, so the three letters at the centre of the seven-letter word go.

parts.note: the front of the word, the two letters standing before the cut
its last two, which close up once the middle has gone

explanation.surface: Troubles of the most pitiless kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the only signal the setter gives: one word is both the thing to be gutted and the description of what survives. Woe is among the oldest words in English and now lives almost entirely in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Woes are troubles, and read straight the clue says what they are: worries with the heart taken out of them.

clue.text: Severely criticize cook

definitions.meaning: to put someone over the fire, figuratively, in print or to their face
the method that uses dry heat in an oven or over an open flame

explanation.surface: Telling the person at the stove exactly what you think of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same verb, and the second is so plain that solvers look past it hunting for wordplay. The insult sense is Victorian and long predates the televised celebrity version.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast a person is to attack them fiercely, and to roast a joint is to cook it in dry heat — one verb, two everyday senses.

clue.text: Flowering shrubs from R. E. Dale & Son

indicators.note: From presents the name as the stuff the answer is made out of — a light touch of an instruction, but it still asks for those letters in a different arrangement.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, initials and surname together
three more from the junior partner

explanation.surface: The name on the sign above an old family nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: The ampersand is pure shopfront and takes no part in the letters, which is the trap: only the name either side of it is fodder. The shrub is evergreen, Mediterranean and poisonous in every part.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleanders are the evergreen Mediterranean shrubs with pink or white blooms, so the definition names them by habit and family.
